messages.subject_clean: Question about Interpretation of Path Model with Endogenous Categorical Variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I understand that endogenous binary and categorical variables need to be specified using the "ordered" function (https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html), which subsequently uses diagonally weighted least squares estimation.

My question is how to interpret the resulting coefficients from these models? My initial thinking was that these would be interpreted similar to an ordinal regression coefficient (i.e., reflecting changes in logged odds), but I'm also finding information to suggest that DWLS assumes an underlying continuous distribution, and that the resulting coefficients would be interpreted on this distribution (Edwards et al., 2012).

If I were to fit a path model with a categorical endogenous variable, would I interpret the regression coefficients as changes in odds or as changes in an assumed underlying continuous distribution? If the latter, are there any estimation methods available in lavaan that would permit an interpretation of changes in probability or odds?

Thanks for any help that can be provided!!

Reference: Edwards, M. C., Wirth, R. J., Houts, C. R., & Xi, N. (2012). Categorical data in the structural equation modeling framework. In R. H. Hoyle (Ed.), Handbook of structural equation modeling. (pp. 195-208). New York, NY, US: The Guilford Press.

If a model with 150 observed variables loading on 6 factors is conventionally specified, there would be more than 300 parameters to estimate from only 200 incomplete observations. I would expect that instability in the covariance matrix of the 150 observed variables--a matrix with 11,325 distinct elements.--would be so great that it would be risky to infer anything from the results. It is impressive that you have an average of 150 / 6 = 25 observed variables per common factor. My guess is that you could put more confidence in results from summing the (standardized) indicators to form 6 composites.

messages.subject_clean: Model Identification and Sample Size
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The error is about the variance-covariance matrix of estimates, not sample covariance matrix. If your sample covariance matrix is not positive definite, most SEM estimators cannot even give you estimates. If you want to check with det() and eigen() you can check the VCOV that Lavaan provides.

Changing the estimator will not help with this problem. Only reducing the estimated parameters will.

If you have many indicators, going with MLR is a safe bet in most situations. See

Rhemtulla, M., Brosseau-Liard, P. É., & Savalei, V. (2012). When can categorical variables be treated as continuous? A comparison of robust continuous and categorical SEM estimation methods under suboptimal conditions. Psychological Methods, 17(3), 354–373.  http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0029315

Mikko

The standard, textbook recommendation for your case is to increase the sample size so that you can actually estimate the original model.

Mikko

messages.body_plain:
> I want to use latent factor residual/error term to predict another latent factor, can we do that in lavaan?

Yes, just define an orthogonal factor that "absorbs" all the residual variance, by setting the residual variance to zero.

model <- ' # latent variable definitions ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 dem60 =~ y1 + a*y2 + b*y3 + c*y4 dem65 =~ y5 + a*y6 + b*y7 + c*y8 # regress mediator on predictor dem60 ~ ind60 # define factor for mediator-residual dem60r =~ 1*dem60
dem60r ~~ 0*ind60 + 0*dem65 # orthogonal to other factors dem60 ~~ 0*dem60 # set variance of "automatic" residual to 0
# regress outcome on mediator-residual
dem65 ~ dem60r ' fit <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)

Be careful about your interpretation.  The results could be quite misleading, depending on what your model is doing.

messages.subject_clean: Comparing non-nested models
messages.body_plain:
> I understand that the limitation of this approach is that I am treating the factor scores as observed variables, meaning that measurement error is not taken into account

No, factor scores are expected to be free of measurement error.  But treating them as observations does not account for sampling error.

Factor indeterminacy is also an issue.

> is it possible to compare these two mediation models with same endogenous, but different exogenous variables?

No, because one set of exogenous predictors is not a subset of the other.  Both of these are nested in a more general model that includes all predictors:

Outcome2 ~ p + c + Outcome1 + control1 + control2 + Int + Ext + Int1 + Ext1 + WB
Outcome1 ~ p + c +            control1 + control2 + Int + Ext + Int1 + Ext1 + WB

Each of your 2 models set some of these coefficients to 0.  What you could do is use Vuong's LRT for nonnested model comparison.  Doing so would require fitting a model that includes all variables, but sets some coefficients to zero.  For example, your med_model1 is

Outcome2 ~ p + 0*c + Outcome1 + control1 + control2 + Int + Ext + 0*Int1 + 0*Ext1 + 0*WB
Outcome1 ~ p + 0*c +            control1 + control2 + Int + Ext + 0*Int1 + 0*Ext1 + 0*WB

Vuong's test is available in the nonnest2 package.

Terrence D. Jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Why independence model handle covariances as free parameters when fixed.x = FALSE ?
messages.subject_clean: Why independence model handle covariances as free parameters when fixed.x = FALSE ?
messages.body_plain:
> The definition of the independence model that I learned from some introductory-level textbooks is a model that assumes that there is no covariance between variables (therefore it estimates only variances).

Yes, among endogenous variables.  It was proposed in the context of "full SEM" (really, the first incremental fit index was developed for factor analysis), not path analysis among observed variables.  Most authors don't explain this very carefully when they make overgeneralizing statements about the independence model.

> However, when a model is fitted with fixed.x = FALSE (i.e. model estimates variances and covariances) the independence model seems to estimate covariances, and those covariances are counted as free parameters.

This has nothing to do with fixed.x=FALSE.  Those covariances will be nonzero by default even when fixed.x=TRUE.  I don't have access to your data, so here is a reprex:

library(lavaan)

## Fit regression model twice, treating exogenous variables as fixed or random variables:

fitF <- sem(model = 'x1 ~ x2 + x3', data = HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x = FALSE)
fitT <- sem(model = 'x1 ~ x2 + x3', data = HolzingerSwineford1939, fixed.x = TRUE)

In the first case, the predictors are considered random variables, so their (co)variances are estimated, as indicated by nonzero numbers in the $free column

data.frame(lav_partable_independence(fitF))

  id lhs op rhs user block group free   ustart exo

1  1  x1 ~~  x1    1     1     1    1 1.358370   0
2  2  x2 ~~  x2    1     1     1    2 1.381784   0
3  3  x3 ~~  x3    1     1     1    3 1.274865   0
4  4  x2 ~~  x3    1     1     1    4       NA   0

In the second case, the predictors are considered fixed variables, so their (co)variances are not estimated, as indicated by zeros in the $free column (and ones in the $exo column).  Instead, those values (both variances and the covariance) are fixed to their observed (nonzero!) sample statistics, reflecting the assumption that in any future replication of this study, the same summary statistics would be observed due to using the same sampling methodology.

data.frame(lav_partable_independence(fitT))

  id lhs op rhs user block group free    ustart exo

1  1  x1 ~~  x1    1     1     1    1 1.3583698   0
2  2  x2 ~~  x2    1     1     1    0 1.3817839   1
3  3  x3 ~~  x3    1     1     1    0 1.2748649   1
4  4  x2 ~~  x3    1     1     1    0 0.4510639   1

The reason that observed predictors' covariances can be nonzero (whether estimated or fixed) in the independence model is that there are typically no hypotheses about those parameters.  By definition, exogenous variables are not explained in the model (they only do the explaining), so it would be inconsistent to place those restrictions in a "worst fitting, but still theoretically defensible" model.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Hi Bram,

I am not familiar with the topic, but from the statistical point of view, I can make the following observations:
1.You might try to use missing = "pairwise" to include units with missing values.
2. & 2. (you have bullet 2. twice). This would indicate a haywood case i.e., there is something wrong with the estimation model. There are no simple answers here. You have to figure out why this occurs (e.g., try removing the variables and changing the model to see what configuration produces this and then try to interpret why this is the case). Maybe you could obtain the residualBM in another analysis (e.g., regression analysis) and then use only the residuals in this analysis. Would probably simplify the model.

The bottom line is that you should not interpret the results of the current model. Revisions are needed.

If a researcher has an indistinguishable dyadic design, they will need to apply a set of constraints and adjust the fit of the model (Kashy et al., 2008; Olsen & Kenny, 2006).

The first set of constraints is that the two means of the latent intercepts and the two means of the latent slopes need to be set equal. (both are latent)

Another set of constraints is that the variances of the intercepts, the slopes (both are latent), and the residuals (of the observed variables) need to be set equal across the two dyad members.

ordered=TRUE just means you want lavaan to treat all observed variables as ordinal, which has nothing to do with missing data.  The default will be DWLS estimation (WLSMV) with listwise deletion, but you can optionally set missing = "pairwise"

> OPTION 2) cfa(specified_model, data = nameofdataset, sampling.weights = "wgt_scaled", std.lv <http://std.lv> = F, meanstructure = T, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ml"). However, the scale is not really symmetric...

Symmetry is not the issue.  There are only 4 possible values, so data cannot really follow a normal distribution.  MLR will adjust for excess kurtosis (the real problem) if you want to pretend your data are continuous, which will not really affect your structural parameters. So this is an option if you want to use FIML and your modeled variables can justify your MAR assumption.

Why does this example (and the next) have sampling weights, yet your first example does not?  Perhaps because lavaan cannot apply sampling weights when using the latent-response assumption (ordered=TRUE), only when data are continuous.

> OPTION 3) cfa (specified_model, data = nameofdataset, sampling.weights = "wgt_scaled", std.lv <http://std.lv> = F, meanstructure = T, estimator = "WLSMV").

I don't see what you think the advantage would be of using DWLS estimation when treating your data as continuous.

Another option is pairwise ML, for which there are additional missing= options listed in the ?lavOptions help page.  Find details here:

https://doi.org/10.1111/bmsp.12243

The paper has lavaan syntax examples in their Supporting Information document linked in the paper.

The latent intercept and latent slope are variables.  Each of them has an intercept and a variance.  Follow the links to see how to specify them.

> The first set of constraints is that the two means of the latent intercepts and the two means of the latent slopes need to be set equal. (both are latent)

For example:

ip1 ~ mean_int*1
ip2 ~ mean_int*1

> Another set of constraints is that the variances of the intercepts, the slopes (both are latent), and the residuals (of the observed variables) need to be set equal across the two dyad members.

For example:

ip1 ~~ var_int*ip1
ip2 ~~ var_int*ip2

> A final set of constraints is that the intra-person and inter-person associations between the intercept and slope factors are set
> equal for both partners. (these are estimated automatically by lavaan, so I don't know how to constrain them).

You just have to specify them in your syntax.

## intraperson
ip1 ~~ i_s_Cov_intra*sp1
ip2 ~~ i_s_Cov_intra*sp2
## interperson
ip1 ~~ i_s_Cov_inter*sp2
ip2 ~~ i_s_Cov_inter*sp1

Also estimate interpersonal correlations of indicators:

PSS.1.00 ~~ PSS.2.00

And set the residual variances equal across partners:

PSS.1.00 ~~ evar1*PSS.1.00
PSS.2.00 ~~ evar1*PSS.2.00

Only simple growth models.

For anything more complex, just specify your model parameters in the syntax and use the lavaan() function instead of a shortcut that doesn't work for your situation.

Hi Terrence,

Thank you very much for your responses. Good to know that we have been running growth models with orthogonal polynomials correctly!

Response 1:
==================================================================================================

Of course, you don't need to model all higher-order polynomials, but if you do, then you will have a saturated model and can test whether something more complex than cubic is required to fit the data well.

==================================================================================================
My response to this suggestion is that: as we only have six time points of data, it may not be adequate to model a quartic growth term and possibly have an overparameterization issue. If this assumption does not make sense, please correct me, thanks!

Response 2:
==================================================================================================

I don't know whose expectation you want to meet, but if you want the intercept to be the mean at the first occasion, then you cannot have orthogonal polynomial contrasts.  Contrasts have means of zero by definition, and any pair of contrasts are orthogonal/uncorrelated because their products have means of zero.  Interpreting the usual intercept as "initial status" is just something you give up when you define growth factors as polynomial contrasts.

For this issue, I understand that the interpretations of intercepts change after defining growth factors as polynomial contrasts. Not sure why you would want to do that, it doesn't seem like a good idea. Also, how are you planning to do it, by applying a threshold? In any case, I understand that the answer to your question is "yes, you should use `ordered = TRUE`" if all your observable variables are turned into categorical.

> 2) if i keep using mix variables, how to make lavvan Identify whether this variable is actually dummy variables or continoous variables.

>From the `lavaan` help page:

ordered

Character vector. Only used if the data is in a data.frame. Treat these variables as ordered (ordinal) variables, if they are endogenous in the model. Importantly, all other variables will be treated as numeric (unless they are declared as ordered in the data.frame.) Since 0.6-4, ordered can also be logical. If TRUE, all observed endogenous variables are treated as ordered (ordinal). If FALSE, all observed endogenous variables are considered to be numeric (again, unless they are declared as ordered in the data.frame.)

That is, you have several options:
Make sure your "dummy" variables are of type `ordered` your data.frame.
Declare the "dummy" ones as ordered by variable name, using a character vector, in the `ordered` argument to lavaan.
Declare the "dummy" ones as ordered by position using a logical vector, in the `ordered` argument to lavaan (where a `TRUE` value means that a variable in that position is to be treated as ordinal, and `FALSE` that it is to be treated as numerical).

> 3) my sample size is more than 5000, which estimator is suitable for this kind of mix variables model.

I understand your sample size is big enough to not be a limiting factor. You should consider other criteria to decide the best estimator.

messages.body_plain:
Let's say your data.frame contains the following variables: `probe_1`, `probe_2`, `diagnostic_1`, `diagnostic_2`. Let's assume `probe_1` and `probe_2` are quantitative variables, and `diagnostic_1` and `diagnostic_2` are dichotomous variables with values " 1=with such disease, 0=without such disease". Then, in your call to `lavaan()` or `cfa()`, you can add the argument:

`ordered = c("diagnostic_1", "diagnostic_1")`

This of course assuming all the variables in your data frame are numeric (including the first two ones). If you don't know what I mean by "numeric variables", you probably need to get a better understanding of the basics of data types in R. I suggest a Google search with precisely the terms data types in R "data types R".

Hope this helps!

messages.subject_clean: How to interpret EFA factor correlation matrix significance
messages.body_plain:
If you're calculating correlations of single variables, the only thing you need to determine the p-value of the correlation is the magnitude of the correlation and the sample size.

When you're working with latent variables (factors) it's more complex, because there's more than that going into the calculation of the standard error.

For example, when you do correlations with single variables, the reliability of the variable affects the correlation - the higher the reliability, the higher the correlation will be (imagine you measured two variables with 0 reliability - your correlation will be zero). You could calculate the attenuation corrected correlation coefficient - you'd say "Well, I found a correlation of 0.3, but my variables are not perfectly reliable, so when I correct the correlations for attenuation, I get 0.5", so the same magnitude of correlation (which might have the same p-value) will lead to different attenuation corrected correlations, and therefore have the same p-values but now the correlations are different.

It's worse than that though - the reliability estimates also have a standard error and so this will feed into the standard error of the corrected correlation. And then there are things like correlated errors - a model might give you an estimate, but if it's not identified, it's standard error will be infinity.  You don't need to go that extreme though - adding a correlation in one part of a model could change the estimates, or the p-values, or both (or neither) of any part of the model.

In short, these aren't inconsistencies. They are expected. You interpret the statistical significance in the same way that you interpret the significance of any other parameter in the model.

Jeremy

I am running a two-group measurement invariance investigation. I have 3 latent factors, each of which has 9 indictors (total number indictors is 27). Jason

On Wed, Jan 17, 2024 at 7:20 AM Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > My model is a growth model, so I need to set constraints on the latent intercept and variance because of the dyadic nature of the data.
>
> The latent intercept and latent slope are variables.  Each of them has an intercept and a variance.  Follow the links to see how to specify them.
>
> > The first set of constraints is that the two means of the latent intercepts and the two means of the latent slopes need to be set equal. (both are latent)
>
> For example:
>
> ip1 ~ mean_int*1
> ip2 ~ mean_int*1
>
> > Another set of constraints is that the variances of the intercepts, the slopes (both are latent), and the residuals (of the observed variables) need to be set equal across the two dyad members.
>
> For example:
>
> ip1 ~~ var_int*ip1
> ip2 ~~ var_int*ip2
>
> > A final set of constraints is that the intra-person and inter-person associations between the intercept and slope factors are set
> > equal for both partners. (these are estimated automatically by lavaan, so I don't know how to constrain them).
>
> You just have to specify them in your syntax.
>
> ## intraperson
> ip1 ~~ i_s_Cov_intra*sp1
> ip2 ~~ i_s_Cov_intra*sp2
> ## interperson
> ip1 ~~ i_s_Cov_inter*sp2
> ip2 ~~ i_s_Cov_inter*sp1
>
> Also estimate interpersonal correlations of indicators:
>
> PSS.1.00 ~~ PSS.2.00
>
> And set the residual variances equal across partners:
>
> PSS.1.00 ~~ evar1*PSS.1.00
> PSS.2.00 ~~ evar1*PSS.2.00
>
> > I'm still quite new to R, but I think the "growth" script is designed to help estimate growth models easily
>
> Only simple growth models.
>
> > but then makes it difficult to make adjustments when the dyadic growth model is employed
>
> For anything more complex, just specify your model parameters in the syntax and use the lavaan() function instead of a shortcut that doesn't work for your situation.

messages.body_plain:
The models are fitted to different data, which should lead to an error even if the df were to differ.  The model with the additional Level-2 predictor "Total" is attempting to reproduce a 3 x 3 Level-2 covariance matrix, whereas the model without "Total" is attempting to reproduce a 2 x 2 Level-2 covariance matrix.  When you add "Total", there are 3 more elements in the 3 x 3 Level-2 covariance matrix (variance of Total, and its 2 covariances with the other 2 variables).  However, the models have the same df because the larger model estimates 3 additional parameters (the slope of Total on the DV, the variance of Total, and its covariance with the other predictor).

messages.body_plain:
Second error first: When you fit a model:
 - all variances should be positive (a variance is a sum of squares)
 - In order to make the model fit, it needs to have a negative variance. This can't exist, so it knows the model is wrong. But it's the best that lavaan can do. Your model is (probably) wrong.

First error is trickier. Lavaan thinks the model is not identified, but it's not sure. The way to be sure is to give the model different starting values. It it doesn't converge to the same place, it's not identified. Identification is a bit tricky - your model is vast, so I'm not surprised that there are issues.

You might try fitting one factor at  a time.

What estimator are you using? Something like ML will be faster than WLS.

Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
You can apply the iht() function to evaluate the order restricted hypothesis using hypothesis testing.
It calls the bootstrapD() function designed for lavaan objects. This results in two hypothesis tests, often referred to as Type A and Type B, as detailed in 10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01565. However, it does not directly answer whether the order-restricted hypothesis holds in the population.
Moreover, the iht method is really slow for lavaan objects because it needs a double bootstrap procedure. You can speed things up using the parallel option, but
still don't be afraid to go on a short holiday.

h1 <- 'a1 > a2 > a3; b1 > b2 > b3'

model <- '

  y1 ~ 1 + a1*x1 + b1*x2
  y2 ~ 1 + a2*x1 + b2*x2
  y3 ~ 1 + a3*x1 + b3*x2
'

iht(model = model, data = PoliticalDemocracy, constraints = h1,
    R = 1000, double.bootstrap = "no", parallel = "snow", ncpus = 8)

The advantage of the goric(a) is that you can directly evaluate your order-restricted hypothesis against its complement (i.e., not h1).

fit.lav <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
goric(fit.lav, hypotheses = list(h1 = h1), comparison = "complement")

>From the results you can conclude that hypothesis h1 is 'some value' more supported than its complement.
See the Vignette in restriktor for "Guidelines interpretation GORIC(A) output" or feel free to contact me.

Leonard
